summary: Béla Bartók was a Hungarian composer, pianist and founding ethnomusicologist who recorded folk songs with Zoltán Kodály. He is best known for the Concerto for Orchestra, with its "Game of Pairs" and Leningrad-parodying "Intermezzo interrotto", Music for Strings, Percussion, and Celesta, the opera Duke Bluebeard's Castle, the ballet The Miraculous Mandarin, the 153-piece Mikrokosmos and six string quartets. His trademarks include eerie "night music", arch form and snap "Bartók pizzicato".
comprehensive_summary:
Béla Bartók was a twentieth-century Hungarian composer and pianist, named alongside Franz Liszt and Zoltán Kodály in questions on Hungary; he and Liszt are considered the greatest Hungarian composers. He is also treated as a founder of ethnomusicology. Introduced to folk-song collecting by Zoltán Kodály, he recorded folk songs on an Edison phonograph, sometimes on walking trips, and collected Hungarian, Romanian and Turkish folk music. He sorted Hungarian songs into "old" and "new" styles and later brought his recordings to Columbia University. He devoted himself to composition after hearing the Budapest premiere of Richard Strauss's Also sprach Zarathustra, which with Ein Heldenleben inspired his early symphonic poem Kossuth. His piano students included Fritz Reiner and Georg Solti, and he died of leukemia while finishing his Third Piano Concerto and Viola Concerto. Tibor Serly completed both.

His most-asked work is the Concerto for Orchestra, commissioned by Serge Koussevitzky for the Boston Symphony Orchestra. It is paradoxically named because every section plays like a soloist. Its second movement, the "Game of Pairs", is framed by a snare-drum solo played without snares and sends pairs of bassoons, oboes, clarinets, flutes and muted trumpets through parallel sixths, thirds, sevenths, fifths and seconds. Its fourth-movement "Intermezzo interrotto" parodies the invasion theme of Shostakovich's Leningrad Symphony and quotes "Da geh' ich zu Maxim" from Lehár's The Merry Widow, and its "Elegia" is in his night-music idiom. Music for Strings, Percussion, and Celesta, written in 1936 for Paul Sacher's Basel Chamber Orchestra, omits winds and divides its players into two antiphonal groups. It opens with a fugue on A that spreads both ways around the circle of fifths to an E-flat climax. Its third-movement Adagio, with a Fibonacci-rhythm xylophone solo and timpani glissandi, was used in Stanley Kubrick's The Shining.

His stage works are the opera Duke Bluebeard's Castle and two ballets. In the opera, Judith forces Bluebeard to open seven doors, revealing a torture chamber, an armory and a lake of tears and, finally, his three former wives, while a minor-second "blood motif" marks each sight of blood. In The Miraculous Mandarin, tramps use a girl to lure a rich Chinese man who survives stabbing and hanging until her embrace lets him die. In The Wooden Prince, a princess loves a staff dressed in a cloak and crown. Cantata Profana sets a Romanian colinda about nine sons turned into stags.

The six string quartets are packed with extended techniques. No. 1 is tied to Stefi Geyer and was called a "return to life" by Kodály. Nos. 4 and 5 use arch form, and No. 4's fourth movement is entirely in the snap "Bartók pizzicato". No. 5 has a Scherzo alla bulgarese in 4+2+3/8, and each movement of No. 6 begins Mesto. His "night music", the eerie nature-imitating texture of his slow movements, takes its name from "The Night's Music" in the 1926 piano suite Out of Doors. That suite was written in his "piano year" alongside the Piano Sonata and the First Piano Concerto. For piano he also wrote the 153-piece graded Mikrokosmos, written for his son Peter and ending with "Six Dances in Bulgarian Rhythm", along with Allegro barbaro and Romanian Folk Dances. Benny Goodman commissioned the verbunkos-opening trio Contrasts, and the Sonata for Two Pianos and Percussion became the concerto of his final public appearance. His influence runs through Ligeti, George Crumb's Makrokosmos and Gunther Schuller's Third Stream.

works.name: String Quartets
works.description: Bartók's six string quartets (1908–1939) are ranked with Shostakovich's fifteen as the foremost twentieth-century sets and are packed with extended techniques.
